source_population_rule: Only exact source records actually supporting the frozen report or property ledger are included. Unused discovery records are excluded.
syntax_normalisation: UTF-8 JSON, two-space indentation, LF line endings and preserved key order; no semantic changes after research freeze.

sources.exact_title: Security Controls for Computer Systems: Report of Defense Science Board Task Force on Computer Security
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Foreword; Parts I–III; especially discussion of system, personnel, physical, communications and procedural safeguards
sources.claim_supported: Early computer security was treated as a whole-system problem involving policy, people, physical environment, communications and technical mechanisms.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: None stated by this source; limitations are recorded in the report and property ledger.

sources.exact_title: Computer Security Technology Planning Study, Volume I
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: pp. 6, 16–20: malicious-user premise, reference monitor, tamper resistance, complete invocation, analysability and environmental assumptions
sources.claim_supported: The reference-monitor conception required mediation of every relevant access, tamper resistance and a size/structure amenable to analysis and testing, under explicit authentication, physical, communications and hardware assumptions.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: None stated by this source; limitations are recorded in the report and property ledger.

sources.author_or_organisation: Jerome H. Saltzer and Michael D. Schroeder
sources.exact_title: The Protection of Information in Computer Systems
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Section IV, pp. 1278–1282: economy, fail-safe defaults, complete mediation, open design, separation of privilege, least privilege, least common mechanism, psychological acceptability
sources.claim_supported: Classic principles identify distinct mechanisms and failure paths; they are not a generic checklist and include usability and common-mechanism constraints.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: None stated by this source; limitations are recorded in the report and property ledger.

sources.author_or_organisation: D. Elliott Bell and Leonard J. LaPadula
sources.exact_title: Secure Computer System: Unified Exposition and Multics Interpretation
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Model statement and concluding discussion, including the Multics interpretation and acknowledgement that the construction is not the unique solution
sources.claim_supported: Bell–LaPadula formalised confidentiality-oriented mandatory access control under a specific state-transition model; it did not constitute a complete general security architecture.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The report itself bounds the model to a particular policy/interpretation and does not establish completeness for integrity, availability or deployment reality.

sources.exact_title: Integrity Considerations for Secure Computer Systems
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Abstract; Sections 2–4 on integrity policies and access constraints
sources.claim_supported: Integrity required models distinct from confidentiality, including constraints intended to prevent improper modification and contamination.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: None stated by this source; limitations are recorded in the report and property ledger.

sources.author_or_organisation: David D. Clark and David R. Wilson
sources.exact_title: A Comparison of Commercial and Military Computer Security Policies
sources.date_version_or_edition: 1987 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Sections on well-formed transactions, transformation procedures, constrained data items and separation of duty
sources.claim_supported: Commercial integrity concerns motivated well-formed transactions, constrained transformation and separation of duty rather than direct reuse of military confidentiality models.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: None stated by this source; limitations are recorded in the report and property ledger.

sources.author_or_organisation: Jack B. Dennis and Earl C. Van Horn
sources.exact_title: Programming Semantics for Multiprogrammed Computations
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Sections on capabilities, access control and protected objects
sources.claim_supported: Capability-style authority linked possession of protected references to operations on objects, contributing a distinct authority lineage.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: None stated by this source; limitations are recorded in the report and property ledger.

sources.exact_title: Protection
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Access matrix, domains, protected objects and confinement discussion
sources.claim_supported: Protection was framed as controlling the use and dissemination of information by subjects over objects, with explicit domains and access rights.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: None stated by this source; limitations are recorded in the report and property ledger.

sources.exact_title: Trusted Computer System Evaluation Criteria (TCSEC, “Orange Book”)
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Divisions D–A; requirements for discretionary/mandatory controls, accountability, assurance and trusted facility management
sources.claim_supported: TCSEC institutionalised security policy and assurance requirements but concentrated on evaluated products and particular confidentiality-oriented assumptions.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Later histories and evaluation practice show limits in portability, compositionality, timeliness and correspondence to deployed configurations.

sources.exact_title: Common Criteria for Information Technology Security Evaluation, Part 1: Introduction and General Model
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Clauses 5–8: TOE, security target, protection profile, assurance and evaluation model
sources.claim_supported: Common Criteria binds evaluation to a defined target of evaluation, security target and assurance package rather than certifying every deployment context.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Evaluation scope, assurance level and configuration can lag operational change; certification is not a universal outcome guarantee.

sources.exact_title: ISO/IEC 15408-1:2026 — Information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection — Evaluation criteria for IT security — Part 1: Introduction and general model
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Publisher abstract and Part 1 general model
sources.claim_supported: The current international evaluation model retains scoped security targets, evaluation evidence and assurance components.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: A standard establishes a practice model, not comparative proof that certification is the optimal or sufficient implementation.

sources.author_or_organisation: Ravi S. Sandhu, Edward J. Coyne, Hal L. Feinstein and Charles E. Youman
sources.exact_title: Role-Based Access Control Models
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Core, hierarchical and constrained RBAC models
sources.claim_supported: RBAC separated permissions from individual identities through organisational roles and constraints, while leaving role engineering and current entitlement as operational burdens.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Role assignment can become stale, over-broad or detached from current parameters; the model does not itself prove least privilege.

sources.author_or_organisation: Vincent C. Hu et al., NIST
sources.exact_title: Guide to Attribute Based Access Control (ABAC) Definition and Considerations
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Sections 2–4: attributes, policy, environment and access-decision model
sources.claim_supported: ABAC made subject, object, action and environmental context explicit in authorisation decisions.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Attribute quality, policy complexity, decision availability and stale context remain preconditions.

sources.author_or_organisation: Auguste Kerckhoffs; transcription/translation hosted by Fabien A. P. Petitcolas
sources.exact_title: La Cryptographie Militaire
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Six principles, especially that compromise of the system design should not require secrecy
sources.claim_supported: Kerckhoffs contributed the open-design lineage: secrecy should be concentrated in manageable keys rather than hidden mechanisms.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: None stated by this source; limitations are recorded in the report and property ledger.

sources.exact_title: Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Whole article; secrecy-system modelling and key/message distinctions
sources.claim_supported: Modern cryptographic systems engineering separates algorithm, key, message and adversary assumptions and supports quantitative reasoning within a model.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: None stated by this source; limitations are recorded in the report and property ledger.

sources.author_or_organisation: Whitfield Diffie and Martin E. Hellman
sources.exact_title: New Directions in Cryptography
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Public-key distribution and authentication discussion
sources.claim_supported: Public-key techniques changed key distribution and authentication architecture but did not remove lifecycle, identity or authority problems.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: None stated by this source; limitations are recorded in the report and property ledger.

sources.exact_title: The Confused Deputy: (or why capabilities might have been invented)
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Confused-deputy example and capability-based resolution
sources.claim_supported: A caller can induce a more privileged service to exercise authority on the caller’s behalf unless authority is explicitly bound to the relevant object and request.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: None stated by this source; limitations are recorded in the report and property ledger.

sources.exact_title: Engineering Trustworthy Secure Systems
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Executive Summary; Chapters 2–3; Annexes E–F
sources.claim_supported: Security is treated as an emergent system property addressed through systems engineering, stakeholder protection needs, assurance and lifecycle evidence.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Guidance establishes an engineering model and vocabulary; it is not comparative proof that every process activity produces better outcomes in every context.

sources.exact_title: Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Executive Summary; Chapters 2–3; Appendix D: anticipate, withstand, recover and adapt
sources.claim_supported: Cyber resilience extends prevention to anticipating, withstanding, recovering from and adapting to adverse conditions while supporting mission objectives.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Resilience claims require concrete mission functions, thresholds and recovery evidence; the vocabulary can otherwise become vague.

sources.author_or_organisation: Murugiah Souppaya, Karen Scarfone and Donna Dodson, NIST
sources.exact_title: Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1: Recommendations for Mitigating the Risk of Software Vulnerabilities
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Practices PO, PS, PW and RV
sources.claim_supported: A secure lifecycle spans organisational preparation, software protection, well-secured production and vulnerability response rather than a single pre-release gate.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The SSDF is outcome/practice guidance and explicitly requires tailoring; conformance alone is not empirical proof of product security.

sources.exact_title: Secure Software Development Practices for Generative AI and Dual-Use Foundation Models: An SSDF Community Profile
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: AI-specific additions across Prepare, Protect, Produce and Respond
sources.claim_supported: AI security is a domain translation of lifecycle engineering with additional model/data/provenance and abuse assumptions, not a replacement for general secure development.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The profile is guidance for an evolving domain; comparative outcome evidence remains limited.

sources.exact_title: Zero Trust Architecture
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Sections 2–3, especially resource protection, per-request access decisions and no implicit trust from network location
sources.claim_supported: Zero trust’s transferable core is granular, resource-specific and continuously evaluated access rather than literal absence of trust.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The architecture depends on policy, identity, telemetry and control-plane availability; it does not make trust assumptions disappear.

sources.author_or_organisation: Ramaswamy Chandramouli and Scott Rose, NIST
sources.exact_title: A Zero Trust Architecture Model for Access Control in Cloud-Native Applications in Multi-Location Environments
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Cloud-native policy, identity, service mesh and enforcement architecture
sources.claim_supported: Workload identity and application/service policy translate current authorisation into distributed cloud-native environments.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Policy distribution and control-plane dependencies create complexity and common-mode risk.

sources.author_or_organisation: NIST National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence
sources.exact_title: Implementing a Zero Trust Architecture
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Executive Summary; Architecture; Builds; Lessons Learned
sources.claim_supported: Real implementations require policy decision/enforcement points, identity and context sources, staged migration and continuing improvement; examples are not a compliance specification.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Every-request or real-time re-evaluation may be costly; interoperability, legacy integration and control-plane failure remain constraints.

sources.exact_title: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Core Functions Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover; Profiles and Tiers
sources.claim_supported: Security outcomes include governance, prevention, detection, response and recovery; the framework is intentionally non-prescriptive.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Framework mapping and maturity descriptions do not by themselves demonstrate outcome effectiveness.

sources.exact_title: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations
sources.date_version_or_edition: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, September 2020; updates through 2025
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Control families AC, AU, CA, CM, CP, IA, IR, RA, SA, SC, SI and SR
sources.claim_supported: The catalogue supplies selectable control outcomes and enhancements across lifecycle and system concerns.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: A control catalogue is not a security argument; selected controls require tailoring, implementation evidence and current assessment.

sources.exact_title: Assessing Security and Privacy Controls in Information Systems and Organizations
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Assessment methods Examine, Interview and Test; assessment-objective and evidence guidance
sources.claim_supported: Assessment must specify objectives, methods, depth, coverage and evidence rather than infer security from control presence.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Assessment remains assumption- and configuration-sensitive and can become ceremonial when evidence is stale or scope is narrow.

sources.author_or_organisation: Murugiah Souppaya and Karen Scarfone, NIST
sources.exact_title: Guide to Enterprise Patch Management Planning: Preventive Maintenance for an Organization’s Technology
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Sections 2–4: identify, prioritise, acquire, install and verify patches; mission and operational trade-offs
sources.claim_supported: Patch management is a lifecycle and risk-balancing process that includes verification, not merely ticket closure or version claims.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Urgent patching can introduce regression and availability risk; delayed patching preserves exposure.

sources.exact_title: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management: A CSF 2.0 Community Profile
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Incident response profile across Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover
sources.claim_supported: Incident response is integrated with risk management and lifecycle preparation rather than beginning only after an alert.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Plans and playbooks require exercises and current authority; documentation alone does not prove response capability.

sources.exact_title: Guide for Cybersecurity Event Recovery
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Recovery planning, playbooks, testing, communications, improvement and metrics
sources.claim_supported: Recovery capability requires preparation, prioritisation, testing and feedback, not merely the existence of backups.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Recovery evidence can go stale and backups can reproduce compromised state.

sources.author_or_organisation: Karen Kent and Murugiah Souppaya, NIST
sources.exact_title: Guide to Computer Security Log Management
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Sections 2–4; privacy and security concerns; infrastructure, planning and operational processes
sources.claim_supported: Security logs support detection, investigation and accountability but introduce storage, access, privacy and sensitive-data risks.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Logging without coverage, integrity, analysis capacity or privacy controls can produce alert fatigue and new exposure.

sources.exact_title: Guide for Security-Focused Configuration Management of Information Systems
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Security-focused configuration management, baselines, change control and monitoring
sources.claim_supported: Security claims must track authorised baselines, actual configuration, changes and deviations.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Baseline compliance can be detached from runtime authority, mission need and current threat.

sources.exact_title: National Checklist Program for IT Products: Guidelines for Checklist Users and Developers
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Checklist selection, evaluation/testing, automation, continuous posture and deviation monitoring
sources.claim_supported: Hardening checklists are contextual inputs whose applicability, testing and current-state monitoring matter more than raw checklist completion.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: A checklist can create false assurance if the environment differs or operational overrides are unobserved.

sources.exact_title: Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management Practices for Systems and Organizations
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Executive Summary; multilevel C-SCRM; supplier, provenance, acquisition and monitoring practices
sources.claim_supported: Supply-chain security requires visibility and governance across suppliers, products, services and lifecycle tiers, not one inventory artefact.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The guidance is broad and implementation-intensive; evidence quality depends on supplier transparency and verification.

sources.exact_title: Strategies for the Integration of Software Supply Chain Security in DevSecOps CI/CD Pipelines
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Pipeline stages, software supply-chain controls and SSDF mapping
sources.claim_supported: Supply-chain controls must bind source, build, dependencies, artefacts and deployment in the delivery pipeline.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Not all practices are universal; pipeline controls can share common credentials and tooling and therefore common-mode failure.

sources.exact_title: Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management: Due Diligence Assessment Quick-Start Guide
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Due-diligence factors including foreign ownership/control/influence, provenance, resilience and supply-chain tiers
sources.claim_supported: Current supplier trust requires risk-based due diligence and evidence beyond vendor assertions.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Due diligence reduces uncertainty but cannot prove absence of malicious or latent compromise.

sources.exact_title: Enhanced Security Requirements for Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: 03.08.03E backup reliability/integrity testing; 03.08.04E recovery and reconstitution to a known state
sources.claim_supported: High-adversarial-pressure systems require tested backups and reconstitution to a known state within defined recovery objectives.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: These enhanced requirements are not a universal cheap path and may be disproportionate for low-consequence systems.

sources.exact_title: Digital Identity Guidelines
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Identity proofing, authentication and federation assurance levels; lifecycle and recovery
sources.claim_supported: Identity proofing, authentication and federation are separate assurance problems with context-sensitive levels and recovery obligations.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Identity assurance does not itself establish authorisation for a particular action or current intent.

sources.exact_title: Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: AAL requirements; phishing resistance; authenticator binding, revocation and account recovery
sources.claim_supported: Phishing-resistant authentication and managed authenticator lifecycles reduce reliance on user recognition and persistent reusable secrets.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Authentication strength does not cure over-broad authorisation, compromised endpoints or unsafe recovery channels.

sources.exact_title: Recommendation for Key Management: Part 1 – General
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Key states, generation, storage, use, archival, compromise, revocation and destruction
sources.claim_supported: Cryptographic trust depends on lifecycle management, separation and compromise response, not algorithm selection alone.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Cryptography cannot compensate for false identities, compromised endpoints, unsafe key authority or unavailable recovery.

sources.exact_title: Recommendations for Federal Vulnerability Disclosure Guidelines
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Executive Summary; Sections 2–3; p. 14 footnote on environmental variation in severity
sources.claim_supported: Vulnerability intake requires reporting, validation, coordination, prioritisation, communication and resolution; technical severity may vary by environment.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Disclosure process does not establish exploitability or remediation in the actual deployed system.

sources.exact_title: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Section 1.2; Chapters 2–7: techniques, benefits, limitations, planning and reporting
sources.claim_supported: Technical assessment techniques have distinct purposes, benefits and limitations and must be planned and interpreted within a broader programme.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The guide expressly does not present a comprehensive security testing programme; a test is bounded evidence.

sources.exact_title: Application Container Security Guide
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Sections 2–4: runtime, namespace/resource isolation, images, registries, orchestrators and host risks
sources.claim_supported: A container is not automatically an independent trust boundary; isolation depends on shared kernel/runtime, configuration, host and orchestration controls.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Containerisation can concentrate common-mode risk in hosts, runtimes and orchestrators.

sources.exact_title: Security Strategies for Microservices-based Application Systems
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Microservice authentication, authorisation, service mesh and availability/performance considerations
sources.claim_supported: Microservice decomposition does not by itself reduce blast radius; service identity, policy, dependency and cascading-failure controls are required.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Distribution can enlarge attack surface and operational complexity.

sources.exact_title: Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Chapters 2–6: performance, reliability, safety, architecture, risk and controls
sources.claim_supported: OT security must account for timing, availability, safety, legacy and physical-process consequences.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: IT-style controls can create unsafe or unavailable operation when translated without domain constraints.

sources.exact_title: Shifting the Balance of Cybersecurity Risk: Principles and Approaches for Secure by Design Software
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Principles: ownership of customer security outcomes, radical transparency/accountability and leadership
sources.claim_supported: Secure-by-design shifts responsibility towards manufacturers and defaults rather than relying principally on customers to compensate for preventable weaknesses.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: A pledge or programme label is not evidence that product architecture, defaults or outcomes changed.

sources.exact_title: Product Security Bad Practices
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Enumerated dangerous product practices and scope qualifiers
sources.claim_supported: Some preventable design choices, including unsafe defaults and avoidable classes of memory-safety defects, should be eliminated at the product level.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The guidance deliberately focuses on especially dangerous practices and is not a complete security standard.

sources.exact_title: Secure by Demand Guide: How Software Customers Can Drive a Secure Technology Ecosystem
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Customer questions and evidence concerning defaults, vulnerability handling, logging, identity and secure development
sources.claim_supported: Procurement can demand evidence and product responsibility without treating questionnaire completion as a security outcome.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Supplier answers remain claims unless independently evidenced and configuration-bound.

sources.author_or_organisation: CISA, NSA, FBI and international partners
sources.exact_title: 2026 Minimum Elements for a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Executive Summary; pp. 4–6; Appendices A–B: author/signature, format/version, generation context, tool identity/version, hashes, coverage, updates and unknowns
sources.claim_supported: An SBOM is a machine-processable transparency input whose quality depends on identity, context, coverage, currentness and explicit unknowns.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The document does not claim that an SBOM proves source trust, build integrity, reachability or absence of vulnerabilities.

sources.author_or_organisation: CISA, NSA, FBI and international partners
sources.exact_title: The Case for Memory Safe Roadmaps
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Executive overview and roadmap recommendations
sources.claim_supported: Memory-safe languages can eliminate broad defect classes and shift burden away from repeated detection, but migration must account for legacy and operational constraints.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Memory safety does not address logic, authorisation, supply-chain or configuration defects.

sources.exact_title: Memory Safe Languages: Reducing Vulnerabilities in Modern Software Development
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Benefits, limitations, performance/concurrency considerations and legacy migration
sources.claim_supported: Class elimination is high leverage where feasible, but language migration is not universally practical and does not replace secure design and testing.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Performance, ecosystem, concurrency, interoperability and rewrite risk can make migration disproportionate.

sources.exact_title: ENISA Secure by Design and Default Playbook
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Sections 2–4; p. 17 threat modelling; 22 principles; SME minimum viable approach; release and change evidence
sources.claim_supported: Mature secure-by-design practice is iterative, decision-linked and scalable; threat modelling is not a one-off documentation artefact and STRIDE is illustrative rather than mandatory.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The playbook is guidance and intentionally permits multiple methods; outcome evidence remains implementation-specific.

sources.exact_title: Good Practices for Supply Chain Cybersecurity
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Threat landscape, supplier relations, assurance and lifecycle measures
sources.claim_supported: Supply-chain risk spans suppliers, services, dependencies and organisational relationships and requires continuous treatment.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Guidance cannot remove opacity in lower supply-chain tiers or prove supplier honesty.

sources.author_or_organisation: U.S. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer
sources.exact_title: DoD Enterprise DevSecOps Reference Design
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Pipeline, software factory, continuous authorisation and security activities
sources.claim_supported: DevSecOps operationalises lifecycle feedback and software-factory controls but can create shared-pipeline and toolchain trust concentrations.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: A reference design is not outcome evidence; pipeline automation can mechanise bad policy or stale evidence.

sources.exact_title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 — Information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection — Information security management systems — Requirements
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Clauses 4–10 and Annex A
sources.claim_supported: An information-security management system establishes governance, risk treatment, objectives, operation, evaluation and improvement requirements.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Certification establishes conformity to a scoped management standard, not proof that a system resists a specified adversary.

sources.exact_title: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 — Information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection — Information security controls
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Organisational, people, physical and technological controls
sources.claim_supported: Security controls span socio-technical and technical concerns and require contextual selection.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: A broad control set can become checklist security if implementation, evidence and threat relevance are not established.

sources.exact_title: ISO/IEC 27005:2022 — Information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection — Guidance on managing information security risks
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Risk context, assessment, treatment, communication, monitoring and review
sources.claim_supported: Security risk decisions require context, consequences, uncertainty, treatment and review rather than severity scores alone.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Risk techniques can create false precision when data and causal models are weak.

sources.exact_title: ISO/IEC 27034-1:2011 — Information technology — Security techniques — Application security — Part 1: Overview and concepts
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Application security management process and organisation normative framework
sources.claim_supported: Application security was explicitly placed across organisational and application lifecycles rather than confined to testing.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The standard is older and process-oriented; current cloud and delivery mechanisms require translation.

sources.exact_title: IEC 62443-4-1:2018 — Security for industrial automation and control systems — Part 4-1: Secure product development lifecycle requirements
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Requirements definition, secure design/implementation, verification/validation, defect management, patch management and end of life
sources.claim_supported: Industrial product security requires a lifecycle including patching and end-of-life duties, translated to safety/availability-constrained environments.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Certification or process compliance does not establish safe deployment in a particular control environment.

sources.exact_title: IEC TS 62443-6-2:2025 — Security evaluation methodology for IEC 62443-4-2
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Evaluation method and prerequisite secure development lifecycle
sources.claim_supported: Security evaluation in industrial products is claim- and requirement-bound and does not mandate a single tool.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Evaluation scope and laboratory evidence do not eliminate integration and operational uncertainty.

sources.exact_title: Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) Specification
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Build track levels 1–3; provenance, authenticity and hardened build requirements
sources.claim_supported: Provenance strength depends on who generates/signs it and how resistant the build platform is to tampering; a record alone is not equivalent to a trustworthy build.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: SLSA levels reduce specified threats but do not establish source correctness or eliminate trusted build infrastructure.

sources.exact_title: in-toto: Providing Farm-to-Table Guarantees for Bits and Bytes
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Threat model, layout/link metadata, verification and evaluation against 30 historical supply-chain compromises
sources.claim_supported: Signed, step-wise supply-chain metadata can verify that authorised actors performed required steps and detect classes of process tampering.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The result depends on key custody, authorised-step definitions and truthful/secure functionaries; it does not prove source security.

sources.exact_title: Sigstore: Software Signing for Everybody
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Architecture, ephemeral identities, transparency log and threat model
sources.claim_supported: Identity-bound short-lived signing and transparency can reduce persistent key-management burden and make release events auditable.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Signing verifies a statement by an identity under system assumptions; it does not prove that the source/build/release is benign.

sources.exact_title: Why Do Software Developers Not Sign Their Software? An Empirical Study of Software Signing Practices
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Interviews with 18 practitioners in 13 organisations; technical, organisational and human barriers; missing/erroneous signatures and adoption disagreements
sources.claim_supported: Signing adoption and correctness face socio-technical barriers; signatures are one component of a broader supply-chain security goal.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The interview sample is bounded and does not estimate population-wide causal effects.

sources.exact_title: The Update Framework Specification
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Threat model, role separation, thresholds, expirations, versioning, rollback/freeze/mix-and-match protections and explicit non-goals
sources.claim_supported: Secure updates require role/key separation, freshness, version and rollback protections and compromise recovery; signed content alone is insufficient.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: TUF does not make content safe, guarantee availability or remove repository/key operational risks.

sources.exact_title: Definitions — When is a build reproducible?
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Definition: same source, build environment and instructions permit any party to recreate bit-for-bit identical specified artefacts
sources.claim_supported: Reproducibility enables independent source-to-binary comparison under declared inputs.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: A reproducible build does not establish that the source or toolchain is secure, and matching compromised builders can reproduce malicious output.

sources.author_or_organisation: Eric O'Donoghue, Yvette Hastings, Ernesto Ortiz and A. Redempta Manzi Muneza
sources.exact_title: Software Bill of Materials in Software Supply Chain Security: A Systematic Literature Review
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Review of 40 peer-reviewed studies; application areas, barriers and ISO/IEC 25019:2023 quality-in-use mapping
sources.claim_supported: SBOM adoption can improve transparency but faces quality, maintenance, interoperability, exploitability and cost limitations.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The evidence base is heterogeneous and many reported benefits are prospective rather than causal.

sources.author_or_organisation: Chengjie Wang, Jingzheng Wu, Hao Lyu, Xiang Ling, Tianyue Luo, Yanjun Wu and Chen Zhao
sources.exact_title: A Large Scale Empirical Analysis on the Adherence Gap between Standards and Tools in SBOM
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: 55,444 SBOMs generated by six tools from 3,287 repositories; inter-tool and longitudinal consistency; licence accuracy
sources.claim_supported: Different tools can produce materially inconsistent component inventories and metadata from the same software.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Preprint status and studied ecosystems limit generalisation; exact figures should not be extrapolated to all toolchains.

sources.author_or_organisation: Li Zhou, Marc Dacier and Charalambos Konstantinou
sources.exact_title: A Reality Check on SBOM-based Vulnerability Management: An Empirical Study and A Path Forward
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: 2,414 repositories across four languages; lock-file generation, scanner false positives and function-call reachability pruning
sources.claim_supported: Inventory-to-vulnerability joins can produce extensive false-positive affectedness, and reachability/context materially change prioritisation.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Preprint methods and language/ecosystem coverage bound transferability.

sources.exact_title: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) Quality
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Quality dimensions for completeness, accuracy, timeliness and fitness for use
sources.claim_supported: SBOM value depends on measurable data quality and intended use, not mere existence.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Quality assessment does not itself establish build provenance or exploitability.

sources.exact_title: Common Vulnerability Scoring System Version 4.0: Specification Document
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Base, Threat, Environmental and Supplemental metric groups
sources.claim_supported: CVSS separates intrinsic severity from threat and environmental modifiers.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: A CVSS score is not an organisation’s risk or proof of exploitation.

sources.exact_title: Common Vulnerability Scoring System Version 4.0: User Guide
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Section explaining that the Base score measures severity, not risk
sources.claim_supported: The standard’s own guidance rejects treating the Base score as risk.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: None stated by this source; limitations are recorded in the report and property ledger.

sources.exact_title: Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Catalogue purpose and remediation due dates
sources.claim_supported: Observed exploitation is a high-value prioritisation input for exposed systems but is neither complete nor a full consequence model.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Absence from the catalogue does not imply absence of exploitation; inclusion does not establish local reachability or impact.

sources.exact_title: Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS)
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Probability estimate that a published CVE will be exploited in the wild in the next 30 days
sources.claim_supported: EPSS supplies a time-bounded exploitation-likelihood estimate that can complement severity and exposure.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The model is observational, depends on available data and does not estimate local consequence or all adversary classes.

sources.exact_title: Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS)
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Model construction, validation and prioritisation comparison
sources.claim_supported: Exploit prediction can discriminate better than severity-only prioritisation for its specified outcome and data.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Prediction quality is outcome- and dataset-specific and does not replace asset, reachability or consequence analysis.

sources.exact_title: Comparing Vulnerability Severity and Exploits Using Case-Control Studies
sources.date_version_or_edition: ACM Transactions on Information and System Security 17(1), 2014
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Case-control comparison of CVSS and evidence of exploits/exploitation
sources.claim_supported: High technical severity alone was a poor proxy for observed exploitation and risk-reduction decisions in the studied data.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Historical datasets and market/telemetry coverage bound applicability to current environments.

sources.exact_title: The Heavy Tails of Vulnerability Exploitation
sources.date_version_or_edition: Engineering Secure Software and Systems (ESSoS 2015), LNCS 8978, pp. 133–148
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Entire empirical study; 374 vulnerabilities and 75.7 million observed attack events; especially distribution/concentration analysis
sources.claim_supported: Observed exploitation was highly concentrated in a small subset of vulnerabilities in the studied environment.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Concentration ratios are environment- and period-specific and should not be universalised.

sources.exact_title: Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM) for Federal Information Systems and Organizations
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Continuous-monitoring strategy, metrics, frequencies, status reporting and response
sources.claim_supported: Security status must be observed at frequencies matched to risk and change; periodic assessment alone cannot bind assurance to current state.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Monitoring creates cost, privacy and alert-volume burdens and can reproduce blind spots in sensors and policy.

sources.exact_title: Attack Trees: Modeling Security Threats
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Tree structure, attacker goals, AND/OR decomposition and attributes
sources.claim_supported: Attack trees make attacker goals and alternative paths explicit and permit path-specific reasoning.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Tree completeness and attribute estimates depend on analyst knowledge and current architecture.

sources.author_or_organisation: Guttorm Sindre and Andreas L. Opdahl
sources.exact_title: Eliciting Security Requirements by Misuse Cases
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Misuse-case construct and relationship to use cases/security requirements
sources.claim_supported: Misuse cases connect hostile or unwanted behaviour to system requirements and mitigations.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Scenario enumeration is not complete and can overrepresent salient known threats.

sources.exact_title: Threat Modeling – A Systematic Literature Review
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Review protocol and synthesis of 54 selected papers from 176 candidates
sources.claim_supported: Threat-modelling research contains many methods and applications, with substantial manual work and limited empirical validation.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The review predates some current cloud and AI methods and does not establish ineffectiveness.

sources.author_or_organisation: Harjot Kaur, Carson Powers, Ronald E. Thompson III, Sascha Fahl and Daniel Votipka
sources.exact_title: “Threat modeling is very formal, it’s very technical, and also very hard to do correctly”: Investigating Threat Modeling Practices in Open-Source Software Projects
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: 25 semi-structured interviews; Sections 5–7 on ad hoc practice, overhead, decentralisation, soundness, completeness and currentness
sources.claim_supported: OSS developers often perform lightweight ad hoc threat reasoning; structured methods can impose expertise, coordination and maintenance costs without guaranteed perceived benefit.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The sample is bounded and qualitative; it supports cost/currentness limits rather than rejection of threat modelling.

sources.exact_title: Empirical Evaluation of Security Threats Analysis (STRIDE)
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Controlled descriptive study with 57 master’s students; threat quality, productivity and cost
sources.claim_supported: STRIDE can structure threat elicitation, but evidence is bounded by participant expertise, tasks and method.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Student participants and bounded systems limit external validity.

sources.author_or_organisation: Katja Tuma, Gul Calikli and Riccardo Scandariato
sources.exact_title: Threat Analysis of Software Systems: A Systematic Literature Review
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Review of threat-analysis methods, activities, artefacts and adoption obstacles
sources.claim_supported: Threat-analysis methods vary materially and face usability, scalability and integration obstacles.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Heterogeneity prevents a single effectiveness estimate.

sources.exact_title: State of the Art: Automated Black-Box Web Application Vulnerability Testing
sources.date_version_or_edition: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 2010
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Evaluation of eight black-box scanners against web vulnerabilities
sources.claim_supported: Automated scanners find real classes of defects but differ in coverage and miss material vulnerabilities.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Results concern the studied tools, applications and period; tool performance evolves.

sources.author_or_organisation: Emma Lavens, Pieter Philippaerts and Wouter Joosen
sources.exact_title: A Quantitative Assessment of the Detection Performance of Web Vulnerability Scanners
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Experimental comparison of 24 scanners across 11 web-vulnerability classes
sources.claim_supported: Scanner results vary by tool and vulnerability class; multiple tools do not imply independent coverage.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Benchmark construction and target representativeness constrain generalisation.

sources.author_or_organisation: Huimin Hu, Yingying Wang, Julia Rubin and Michael Pradel
sources.exact_title: An Empirical Study of Suppressed Static Analysis Warnings
sources.date_version_or_edition: Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering 2 (FSE), 2025, pp. 290–311
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: 7,357 suppressions across 46 Python projects; taxonomy and present-warning analysis
sources.claim_supported: Warning suppression reflects false positives, tool/configuration limits, misleading messages and deliberate trade-offs; 50.8% of studied suppressions affected no warning in the analysed current configuration.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The study does not show that static analysis lacks value; precise rules and high-consequence checks can be effective.

sources.author_or_organisation: Zhen Yu Ding and Claire Le Goues
sources.exact_title: An Empirical Study of OSS-Fuzz Bugs
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: 23,907 bugs across 316 projects; bug types, lifecycle, fixing, flakiness and CVE reporting
sources.claim_supported: Continuous fuzzing often finds defects quickly and supports rapid fixes, while flakiness, timeouts, resource failures and weak vulnerability labelling remain limits.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Fuzzing evidence is input- and harness-dependent and cannot establish semantic, authorisation or architectural properties.

sources.exact_title: OSS-Fuzz — Google’s Continuous Fuzzing Service for Open Source Software
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Architecture, continuous integration and initial findings
sources.claim_supported: Continuous fuzzing integrates defect discovery into development rather than relying on one release test.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Service-scale findings are not proof of coverage or absence of bugs.

sources.exact_title: seL4: Formal Verification of an OS Kernel
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Functional-correctness theorem from abstract specification to C implementation; stated assumptions
sources.claim_supported: Machine-checked proof can exhaustively establish a precise implementation/refinement claim within its model and trusted assumptions.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The proof assumes compiler, assembly, boot code, hardware and specification adequacy and does not cover every deployed component or security objective.

sources.exact_title: Verification Assumptions
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Trusted computing base and explicit proof assumptions
sources.claim_supported: A formal assurance claim remains bounded by its trusted assumptions and configuration.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Assumption lists make limits explicit but do not validate the assumptions themselves.

sources.exact_title: Formal Verification of a Realistic Compiler
sources.date_version_or_edition: Communications of the ACM / related POPL account, 2009
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Compiler semantic-preservation theorem and trusted components
sources.claim_supported: Verified compilation can remove a major source of proof-chain uncertainty but remains theorem-, language- and toolchain-scoped.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: It does not prove source-program security or hardware/deployment correctness.

sources.author_or_organisation: Maurice H. ter Beek et al.
sources.exact_title: Formal Methods in Industry
sources.date_version_or_edition: Formal Aspects of Computing 37(1), Article 7; published 26 December 2024
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Sections 2–3; industrial applications; survey-reported barriers to uptake
sources.claim_supported: Formal methods have substantial industrial applications across lifecycle stages and domains, but training, tool maintenance, lifecycle integration and learning cost materially constrain uptake.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The article primarily assembles successful applications and expert testimony; it is not a population-level causal comparison of formally verified and unverified systems.

sources.exact_title: Verification and Test Methods for Access Control Policies/Models
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Model checking, theorem proving, testing and policy verification
sources.claim_supported: Different verification and testing techniques answer different access-control claims and carry distinct assumptions.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: A verified policy model does not establish correct enforcement, identity inputs or deployment configuration.

sources.author_or_organisation: Thomas Maillart, Mingyi Zhao, Jens Grossklags and John Chuang
sources.exact_title: Given Enough Eyeballs, All Bugs Are Shallow? Revisiting Eric Raymond with Bug Bounty Programs
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Vulnerability-discovery distributions and bounded contributions by researchers
sources.claim_supported: Diverse external researchers can contribute non-identical discoveries, but each researcher’s output is bounded and a programme is not exhaustive.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Programme incentives, scope, triage and participant population shape findings.

sources.exact_title: An Empirical Study of Bug Bounty Programs
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Programme characteristics, report outcomes and incentives
sources.claim_supported: Bug bounties can extend discovery but exhibit duplication, invalid reports, incentive and triage burdens.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Observed platform programmes may not represent private or high-assurance environments.

sources.author_or_organisation: Anne Adams and Martina Angela Sasse
sources.exact_title: Users Are Not the Enemy
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Study of password and security behaviour; communication, workload and policy mismatch
sources.claim_supported: User workarounds often reflect unusable policy, poor communication and task conflict rather than irrational hostility to security.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The study is historically specific; authentication technology and work practices have evolved.

sources.exact_title: So Long, and No Thanks for the Externalities: The Rational Rejection of Security Advice by Users
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Cost-benefit analysis of user security advice
sources.claim_supported: Users may rationally reject low-yield advice when recurring compliance cost is imposed on them while benefits are diffuse or rare.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The calculations depend on estimated risks and user populations; the core point is incentive/cost alignment, not universal rejection.

sources.author_or_organisation: Anthony Vance, Jeffrey L. Jenkins, Bonnie Brinton Anderson, Daniel K. Bjornn and C. Brock Kirwan
sources.exact_title: Tuning Out Security Warnings: A Longitudinal Examination of Habituation Through fMRI, Eye Tracking, and Field Experiments
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Five-day fMRI/eye-tracking experiment and three-week mobile field experiment
sources.claim_supported: Repeated, invariant warnings lose attention and can become acknowledgement rituals.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Warning design and context differ; habituation is not the only cause of non-compliance.

sources.exact_title: Understanding the Efficacy of Phishing Training in Practice
sources.date_version_or_edition: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 2025
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Eight-month randomised controlled field experiment; over 19,500 healthcare employees and ten campaigns
sources.claim_supported: Annual and embedded phishing training, as commonly deployed in the studied organisation, produced limited protective effect.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: One large organisation and its training designs do not prove all role-specific or just-in-time training ineffective.

sources.exact_title: Why Information Security is Hard — An Economic Perspective
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Incentive misalignment, externalities, information asymmetry and market structure
sources.claim_supported: Security failure often follows misaligned incentives and concentrated externalities, not merely missing technical controls.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Economic mechanisms explain classes of behaviour but do not replace system-specific technical analysis.

sources.exact_title: What’s Wrong with Risk Matrices?
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Proofs/examples of poor resolution, range compression, non-monotonicity and ranking reversal
sources.claim_supported: Qualitative risk matrices can assign identical labels to different risks and reverse decision orderings.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Carefully bounded ordinal categories may still support communication; the critique targets decision validity and false precision.

sources.author_or_organisation: Frank Cremer, Barry Sheehan, Michael Fortmann, Arash N. Kia, Martin Mullins, Finbarr Murphy and Stefan Materne
sources.exact_title: Cyber Risk and Cybersecurity: A Systematic Review of Data Availability
sources.date_version_or_edition: The Geneva Papers on Risk and Insurance — Issues and Practice 47, 2022, pp. 698–736
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Systematic search of 5,219 studies and characterisation of 79 unique datasets
sources.claim_supported: Cyber-risk quantification is constrained by sparse, biased, incompatible and access-limited incident/loss data.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The review maps data limitations; it does not show quantitative methods are never useful.

sources.author_or_organisation: Steve Lipner and Michael Howard, Microsoft
sources.exact_title: The Trustworthy Computing Security Development Lifecycle
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Mandatory SDL stages, threat modelling, testing, release and response
sources.claim_supported: Microsoft SDL is a historically important deployed secure-development programme linking activities across a product lifecycle.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Programme claims and outcome reductions are partly vendor-reported and do not establish that each mandated activity is independently causal.

sources.exact_title: Security Development Lifecycle
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Current SDL practices and tooling
sources.claim_supported: A major deployed SDL continues to integrate requirements, design, implementation, verification, release and response.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Vendor guidance is implementation evidence, not independent effectiveness evidence.

sources.exact_title: Review of the Summer 2023 Microsoft Exchange Online Intrusion
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Message from the Chair; Findings and Recommendations: cascade of failures in identity/signing-key and cloud security
sources.claim_supported: A high-value cloud compromise resulted from a cascade of identity, key, logging, validation and organisational failures; a central provider became a systemic trust concentration.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Incident evidence strongly establishes mechanisms in this case but does not estimate universal control effectiveness.

sources.exact_title: Review of the December 2021 Log4j Event
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Executive Summary; ecosystem dependence, vulnerability response, asset discovery and long-tail risk
sources.claim_supported: A ubiquitous transitive dependency created systemic exposure, difficult affectedness determination and a long remediation tail.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The event is an extreme case and does not imply every dependency warrants equal process depth.

sources.exact_title: Advanced Persistent Threat Compromise of Government Agencies, Critical Infrastructure, and Private Sector Organizations
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Supply-chain compromise of SolarWinds Orion build/distribution and remediation guidance
sources.claim_supported: Trusted build and update channels can distribute compromise at scale; signed/normal distribution does not prove benign provenance.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Public reporting leaves some mechanism details uncertain; conclusions are bounded to documented facts.

sources.exact_title: Reported Supply Chain Compromise Affecting XZ Utils Data Compression Library (CVE-2024-3094)
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Maintainer/community compromise and affected versions
sources.claim_supported: Long-horizon social and maintainer compromise can bypass ordinary source trust and enter release artefacts.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The malicious versions were detected before broad stable distribution in many ecosystems; it does not show all OSS governance is untrustworthy.

sources.exact_title: Falcon Content Update Preliminary Post Incident Report
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Faulty rapid-response content deployment, validation and system impact
sources.claim_supported: A security update/control can create common-mode availability failure when release validation and staged rollout are inadequate.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Vendor self-reporting may omit independent perspectives; the incident mechanism is nevertheless directly documented.

sources.exact_title: #StopRansomware Guide
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Offline encrypted backups, integrity/availability testing, response and recovery
sources.claim_supported: Recovery from destructive compromise requires separated, tested backups and care to avoid restoring compromised state.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Backups alone do not restore identity, authority, configuration or service trust.

sources.exact_title: Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Lifecycle stages, attacker goals, capabilities, knowledge and mitigations
sources.claim_supported: AI security requires explicit attacker capability, knowledge, lifecycle stage and objective; benchmark labels do not generalise automatically.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: A taxonomy organises claims but does not establish mitigation effectiveness.

sources.exact_title: Guidelines for Secure AI System Development
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Secure design, development, deployment and operation; supply chain, monitoring, updates and incident management
sources.claim_supported: AI systems inherit general lifecycle, provenance, monitoring and response duties while adding model/data-specific concerns.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: The guidance is principles-led and the field’s empirical evidence remains uneven.

sources.exact_title: Cybersecurity in Medical Devices: Quality System Considerations and Content of Premarket Submissions
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Threat modelling, security risk management, architecture, updates, SBOM, monitoring and safety interactions
sources.claim_supported: Medical-device security must be co-engineered with safety, clinical availability, updates and lifecycle evidence.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Regulatory guidance establishes expectations, not proof of comparative optimality or field effectiveness.

sources.exact_title: Security Assurance Requirements for Linux Application Container Deployments
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Container threat scenarios, shared host/runtime dependencies and assurance requirements
sources.claim_supported: Separate processes or containers are not necessarily independent trust boundaries when they share privileged runtime/kernel components.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Specific container technologies and defaults evolve; the shared-dependency principle remains transferable.

sources.exact_title: Zero Trust Maturity Model
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Identity, devices, networks, applications/workloads and data pillars; cross-cutting visibility, automation and governance
sources.claim_supported: Zero-trust implementation is multi-dimensional and staged, not a binary purchase.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Maturity levels are planning constructs, not validated security outcome scores.

sources.exact_title: #StopRansomware: Gunra Ransomware
sources.exact_section_page_table_figure_or_locat: Mitigations including tested offline, immutable and segmented backups
sources.claim_supported: Current defensive guidance continues to require separated, tested recovery material because accessible backups are adversary targets.
sources.contrary_evidence_if_any: Advisory recommendations are threat-specific and do not establish a universal architecture.
